title: Icecream Fitness Program review
summary: NH reviews the first version of Jason Blaha's Icecream Fitness 5x5 novice program, criticising its 12-week length, two alternating full-body days stuffed with compounds, 5x5 on technical lifts, squat and deadlift on the same day, and odd accessory rep schemes. He then reorganises the same template with evolving rep ranges, supersets, and a light squat variation, adding pull-ups and long-head triceps work as suggestions.

claims.claim: Icecream Fitness by Jason Blaha is one of YouTube's best-known novice programs, largely because he spammed it on 4chan and Reddit; promoting a free program is fair but it can still be criticised.
A novice program with a fixed 12-week length makes no sense: beginners aren't peaking for a meet and should stay on a program until it stops working; a program that only works 12 weeks is bad.
Twice per week per lift/muscle is a good frequency for novices.
90-minute workouts are pushing it but acceptable since it isn't two hours.

Men and women shouldn't train identically: different body types, injury tolerance and muscle distribution; YouTube fitness just puts women on men's programs because they're a tiny share of the audience.
Blaha didn't invent the program; it's essentially Madcow 5x5 with accessories added. Combining existing rep schemes and lifts isn't invention, though making a good program is still a skill.

With three training days a week you could have three distinct workouts, allowing fewer exercises per day and room for variations and accessories, instead of repeating two compound-stuffed days forever.

Following squats with bench press wastes time because none of the squat muscles carry over, forcing a full new warm-up; he prefers programs with synergy, e.g. lower days and upper days, and dislikes full bodies.
Squat, bench and row in one session means repeated re-warming, a lot of wasted time even for light novices.
3x8 is too little for traps, which can take much more volume; do something like 3x20 instead.
Resting two minutes after shrugs is unnecessary; isolation work like shrugs should be supersetted.
Straight or EZ-bar curls are great because you can load them heavily; incline curls require low weight, overextend the tendon, and he thinks they are a poor biceps exercise.
5x5 (25 reps) vs 3x8 (24 reps) is nearly the same rep count; tonnage falls on isolation moves only because loads are lighter.
Get quality tonnage from strength work without pushing it too far, and get much, even most, of your tonnage from variations and accessories; it reduces injury and progresses as well or better.
5x5 on bent-over rows is terrible: the row is more technical than people think, novices cheat with lower back and legs, and will never get five clean reps on the last set.
2x10 hyperextensions with a plate is a joke; push volume up (e.g. 4x20). Few sets also tempt novices to go too heavy and ruin technique.
He doesn't dislike cable crunches but never got anything from them; the angle feels weird.
Workout A lacks long-head triceps work, rear and side delt work (only front delts via bench) and upper back, and has no calves.
He gets little lat involvement from bent-over rows.
Novices should focus on basics, but that doesn't mean cramming all the basics into one day with random rep schemes; 5x5 working for novices doesn't make it best.
Squatting 5x5 every session is unnecessary.

Never do heavy squats and heavy deadlifts on the same day; whichever comes second suffers. Pair a heavy version of one with a lighter variation of the other (squat + stiff-leg deadlift, deadlift + pause squat).
1x5 is a great rep scheme for the deadlift: it needs less volume and frequency, and heavy warm-ups already add a lot of tonnage.
5x5 on overhead press is not terrible.
Instead of rowing 10% lighter on day B, a pendlay row variation would have been a better choice than manipulating intensity.
Close-grip bench 3x8 on day B is good: extra horizontal press volume without smoking the shoulders, synergising with day A bench.
Overhead pressing after squats and deadlifts risks a fried lower back and wobbly base, setting novices up to press with poor form.
Full-body workouts can be done right, but most people just slap compound movements together.
Revised day A: squat 5x4-6 and bench 5x4-6; a 4-6 evolving rep range lets you do e.g. 6,6,5,5 and learn to manage volume and intensity.
Revised day A rows: 3-4 sets of 4-8 so you can drop reps to stay clean as form degrades, supersetted with barbell shrugs 3x15-20.
Traps are very resilient and rows only use them a little, so shrugs superset well with rows.
He normally prefers 10-15 reps for isolation, but for novices opens it to 15-20 for a wider evolving range; triceps extensions 3x15-20 supersetted with straight-bar curls 3x8-12.
Finish day A with hyperextensions 3x15-20 supersetted with any ab isolation, e.g. cable crunches 3x15-20.
Supersets save time, raise metabolic and cardiovascular demand, and evolving rep ranges ensure you can always finish the workout instead of failing a fixed scheme.
Revised day B starts with heavy deadlift 1x5, optionally back-off sets of 3x3 at submaximal weight for technique and safe tonnage.
Two strength lifts per workout is plenty; three would be too much.

Revised day B: light squat variation (pause or front squat) 3x8-12 or 3x6-10, overhead press 5x4-6 supersetted with straight-bar curls 5x6-12, rows 3x4-8 supersetted with close-grip bench 3x8, no abs.
Strength work focuses strictly on progress and intensity, not volume; accessories are different.
Supersetting curls with overhead press doesn't hurt pressing ability.
After squats, deadlifts, overhead press and rows you don't need extra ab work.
Strength work should not be supersetted because you want full focus.
The program lacks vertical pulling: add pull-ups at the end, supersetted with any non-strength work.
Add long-head triceps work: swap day A extensions for skull crushers and day B cable crunches for behind-the-head cable extensions.
Ignored body parts matter more once intermediate; novices are building a base and won't stay novices long.
He rebuilt a good program purely by rearranging the given material, showing that people claiming to have created great programs are just recombining notions from books or teachers.
